title: Afraid of dying
message: Fear of death is one of the most human feelings there is, and the Bible does not tell you to pretend otherwise. Jesus himself wept at a friend's grave. The New Testament speaks of Jesus breaking the power of death and freeing "those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death."
step: Read Psalm 23 slowly. Notice that the valley is still dark, but you are not alone in it.

passages.why: "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil."
Jesus at his friend Lazarus's grave: "I am the resurrection and the life."
"Do not let your hearts be troubled... In my Father's house are many rooms."
Jesus came to free people held captive by the fear of death.
"Where, O death, is your sting?"
Nothing, not even death, can separate us from God's love.

options.label: I want to understand what happens

title: Trying to understand death

terms: where do we go when we die

message: People have always asked why we die and what comes after. The Bible treats death as real and painful, something that was not part of God's good beginning. It also holds out the hope that, because Jesus rose from the dead, death is not the end of the story. Christian traditions explain the details in different ways.
step: Read 1 Corinthians 15:20-22 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14, then write down one question you still have.

passages.why: Where death enters the Bible's story: "for dust you are, and to dust you shall return."
"A time to be born and a time to die."
"Teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom."
Christ raised as the "firstfruits" of all who have died.
Grieving, but not "like the rest, who are without hope."
A future where "there will be no more death or mourning."

links.label: What happens when we die? How traditions answer

followUp.question: Is something else behind your question?

title: Grieving someone
message: I'm so sorry. Grief can feel overwhelming, and it often comes with anger, numbness or questions about God. The Bible gives words for all of it: whole psalms are laments, and Jesus wept with his friends at Lazarus's grave. Mourning is not a lack of faith; Jesus said, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted."
step: Read Psalm 34:18. You don't need to find the right words; you can simply tell God what you miss.

passages.why: "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted."
"Jesus wept." He grieved with Mary and Martha.
"Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted."
An honest prayer: "Why are you downcast, O my soul?"
Grief and hope side by side: "His mercies never fail."
"He will wipe away every tear from their eyes."

title: God feels far away
message: Many faithful people have felt that God was distant or silent, and the Bible doesn't hide it. "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" is a prayer in Scripture. Jesus himself cried out on the cross, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" Feeling far from God is not the same as God being far from you.
step: Pray Psalm 13 as your own words, even if you don't feel it yet. It starts in complaint and ends in trust.

passages.why: "How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?" A short prayer that moves from complaint to trust.
"My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" The words Jesus prayed on the cross.
"Where can I flee from Your presence?" Even darkness is not dark to God.
"Can a woman forget her nursing child?... I will not forget you."
The father runs to meet the son who wandered away.
"Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you."

links.label: How to pray when it's hard

followUp.question: What's closest to how you feel?

options.label: My faith feels cold or dry

title: Faith feels cold or lukewarm
message: Seasons where faith feels flat, routine or "lukewarm" are common, even for people who have believed for years. The Bible speaks to this directly, not to shame but to invite: Jesus says, "I stand at the door and knock." Thirst for God can itself be a sign that something is alive.
step: Read Psalm 42:1-2 and then pick one small, honest practice for this week: a short daily reading, a walk where you pray, or meeting with someone you trust.

passages.why: Jesus to a "lukewarm" church: "I stand at the door and knock."
"As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You."
"Restore to me the joy of Your salvation."
"You have abandoned your first love" — a call to return.
"Remain in Me... apart from Me you can do nothing."
Strength renewed for those who wait on the LORD.

title: Feeling worthless
message: If you feel worthless right now, you are in good company in the Bible. One psalm even says, "I am a worm and not a man," and goes on to find that God has not turned away. The Bible's steady message is that your worth comes from being made and loved by God, not from what you achieve or how you feel today.
step: Read Psalm 139:13-16 and say verse 14 out loud, even if you don't believe it yet.

passages.why: "But I am a worm and not a man" — an honest lament that turns to trust.
"I am fearfully and wonderfully made."
"You are precious and honored in My sight, and... I love you."
Not one sparrow is forgotten; "you are worth more than many sparrows."
"Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God."
"We are God's workmanship."

title: New to God and the Bible
chip: New here: where do I start?
message: Welcome. You don't need to know anything to start. The Bible is a library of 66 books, and you don't have to read it front to back. Many people begin with the Gospel of Mark, a short, fast-moving account of Jesus' life, because Christians believe Jesus is the clearest picture of who God is.
step: Read Mark 1 at the "Plain" or "Modern" level. It takes about 10 minutes. Then try the 21-day First Steps plan.

passages.why: The start of the shortest Gospel: Jesus begins his work.
Who Jesus is, in John's poetic opening.
The very beginning: God creates the world and calls it good.
The best-known prayer in the Bible: "The LORD is my shepherd."
Three stories Jesus told about what God is like.

options.label: How do I read the Bible?

title: Who is Jesus?
message: Jesus was a Jewish teacher from Nazareth in the first century, who was crucified in Jerusalem. His followers proclaimed that he rose from the dead and that he is the Messiah, the Son of God. Jesus himself asked his friends, "Who do you say I am?" The Gospels were written so readers could answer that for themselves.
step: Read the Gospel of Mark over a couple of weeks, and keep that question in mind.

passages.why: Jesus asks: "Who do you say I am?"
"The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us."
He "did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many."
"The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost."
"I am the way and the truth and the life."
The early Christian hymn about Jesus humbling himself.

options.label: I'm new: where do I start?

title: How do I read the Bible?
message: The Bible is a collection of 66 books written over about 1,500 years: stories, laws, poems, prophecy and letters. It tells one big story, from creation, through the history of Israel, to Jesus and the early church, and a hope for a renewed world. It helps to know what kind of writing you are reading, and to start with the Gospels.
step: Use the Simplify slider: read a chapter at "Summary", then "Plain", then "Modern". Every book has an introduction card.

passages.why: Jesus explains how the Scriptures point to him.
"All Scripture is God-breathed."
"Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path."
Why John wrote his Gospel.
Reading the Law and explaining it, "so that the people could understand."

links.label: Why Catholic Bibles have more books

title: Anxious or worried
message: Anxiety can be exhausting, in your body as well as your mind. The Bible doesn't say anxious people are failing; it invites them to bring every worry to God, and promises a peace that "surpasses all understanding." If anxiety is affecting your daily life, talking with a doctor or counsellor is wise and good.
step: Read Philippians 4:6-7, then name one worry to God, out loud or on paper, and leave it with him for today.

passages.why: "Be anxious for nothing... and the peace of God... will guard your hearts."
Jesus on worry: look at the birds and the lilies.
"Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you."
"When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul."
"Be still, and know that I am God."
"Peace I leave with you... Do not let your hearts be troubled."

title: Afraid
message: "Do not be afraid" is one of the most repeated phrases in the Bible, and it is almost always said with a reason: "for I am with you." Fear is not a sin; it's a signal. The Bible invites you to bring it to God rather than face it alone.
step: Read Psalm 56:3-4 and use it as a one-line prayer whenever fear rises: "When I am afraid, I put my trust in You."

passages.why: "When I am afraid, I put my trust in You."
"Do not fear, for I am with you."
"The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?"
"Be strong and courageous... the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."
"God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control."
Jesus calms a storm: "Why are you so afraid?"

title: Lonely
message: Loneliness hurts, and the Bible takes it seriously: it says from the start that "it is not good for the man to be alone." One psalm simply prays, "Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted." Jesus promised his friends, "I am with you always," and called his followers to be a family for one another.
step: Read Psalm 25:16-18 as your prayer, and consider one small step to connect with someone this week, perhaps a local church or group.

passages.why: "Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted."
"God settles the lonely in families."
"He will never leave you nor forsake you."
"Surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age."
Jesus: "I have called you friends."
"Two are better than one."

links.label: Find a church tradition that fits

title: Guilty or ashamed
message: Guilt can be heavy. The Bible is honest that everyone has done wrong, and just as honest that God is "compassionate and gracious... abounding in loving devotion." Psalm 51 was written after a terrible wrong, and it is full of hope. Christian traditions practise confession in different ways, but all of them speak of God's forgiveness through Jesus.
step: Pray Psalm 51:1-12 slowly as your own words. Then read 1 John 1:9.

passages.why: "Create in me a clean heart, O God."
"If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us."
"As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us."
"There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
The son comes home ashamed; the father runs to him.
Jesus welcomes a woman known for her sins: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace."

links.label: How can I be right with God?

options.label: How can I be right with God?
I keep giving in to temptation

title: Hurt by someone or struggling to forgive
message: Being hurt by someone is painful, and forgiving can be one of the hardest things anyone is asked to do. The Bible is honest about betrayal, and it calls Christians to forgive as they have been forgiven. Forgiving is not pretending it didn't matter, and it does not mean staying somewhere unsafe. If someone is harming you, your safety comes first.
step: Read Psalm 55:12-14 and 22. Tell God honestly what happened before trying to forgive.

passages.why: "It is not an enemy who insults me... but it is you, a man like myself, my companion."
"Cast your burden upon the LORD, and He will sustain you."
Joseph forgives the brothers who sold him: "What you intended against me for evil, God intended for good."
Peter asks how often to forgive; Jesus answers with a parable.
"Forgive as the Lord forgave you."
"Do not repay anyone evil for evil... Do not avenge yourselves."

title: Angry
message: Anger is a strong emotion, and the Bible doesn't call all anger wrong: Jesus was angry at injustice and hard hearts. It warns about anger that turns into harm or bitterness: "Be angry, yet do not sin." Some of the psalms are even angry prayers, which shows you can bring your anger to God rather than hide it.
step: Read James 1:19-20, then write down what made you angry and give it to God before you act on it.

passages.why: "Be angry, yet do not sin. Do not let the sun set upon your anger."
"Be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger."
"Refrain from anger and abandon wrath."
"A gentle answer turns away wrath."
Jesus is angry at hardness of heart, and heals.
Jonah is angry with God, and God answers him patiently.

options.label: I'm angry at God about suffering

title: Doubts: is any of this true?
message: Doubt is part of many people's faith journey, and the Bible makes room for it. A desperate father said to Jesus, "I do believe; help my unbelief!" Thomas wouldn't believe until he saw for himself, and John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask whether Jesus was really the one. Honest questions are welcome.
step: Read John 20:24-29 and Luke 1:1-4. Write down your biggest question and look for honest answers, including from people who disagree.

passages.why: "I do believe; help my unbelief!"
Thomas asks to see the evidence, and Jesus meets him.
John the Baptist asks, "Are You the One who was to come?"
Luke's careful "orderly account" from eyewitnesses.
Paul lists the witnesses of the risen Jesus.
A believer who nearly lost his footing, and what changed.
"Have mercy on those who doubt."

links.label: Read the book introductions (dates and authors)

title: Why does God allow suffering?
message: This is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and the Bible doesn't give a neat answer. Job's friends offered easy explanations and God said they were wrong. The Bible gives honest laments, the promise that God will one day end all suffering, and Jesus, who suffered with and for us.
step: Read Job 38:1-7 and Job 42:1-6, then Romans 8:18-28. Notice that God answers Job with presence, not a formula.

passages.why: Job loses everything and grieves honestly.
God answers Job "out of the whirlwind."
Jesus rejects the idea that suffering is always someone's fault.
Creation "groaning", and God working for good in all things.
"Our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal glory."
"He will wipe away every tear... Behold, I make all things new."

followUp.question: Is this personal for you right now?

title: Sick or in pain
message: Illness and pain can affect everything: your body, your mood, your faith. The Bible is full of people who cried out to God in sickness, and Jesus spent much of his time with the sick. Christians pray for healing, and also find that God's strength can be with them in weakness. Please keep following the care of your doctors too.
step: Read Psalm 6:2-4 as a prayer, and 2 Corinthians 12:9: "My grace is sufficient for you."

passages.why: "Heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony."
"The LORD will sustain him on his bed of illness."
A woman ill for twelve years reaches out to Jesus.
"Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him."
"My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness."
"He gives power to the faint."

links.label: Are the gifts of the Spirit (like healing) for today?

title: Low, hopeless or depressed
message: I'm sorry you're feeling this way. Depression is real, and it is not a sign of weak faith. The prophet Elijah once lay down and said, "I have had enough, LORD." God's first response was rest and food. Please consider talking to a doctor or someone you trust; reaching out for help is a good and faithful thing to do.
step: Read 1 Kings 19:3-8. Today, the next step might simply be to rest, eat, and tell one person how you are.

passages.why: Elijah: "I have had enough, LORD." God sends rest and food.
"Why are you downcast, O my soul?... Put your hope in God."
The darkest psalm, a prayer that ends in darkness. Even this is in the Bible.
"The LORD is near to the brokenhearted."
Remembering misery, and still hoping.
"Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest."

title: Worn out or exhausted
message: Being worn out is not a failure. God built rest into creation and gave it as a gift. Jesus told his tired disciples, "Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while," and invited the weary to come to him for rest.
step: Read Matthew 11:28-30. Then take one real step to rest this week, and don't feel guilty about it.

passages.why: "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest."
"Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while."
"He makes me lie down in green pastures... He restores my soul."
"They will run and not grow weary."
"He gives sleep to His beloved."
An exhausted prophet is given rest and food.

title: Thankful or joyful
message: Wonderful. The Bible is full of songs of thanks, and gratitude is one of the most natural responses to God. "Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever." Joy is worth savouring and sharing.
step: Read Psalm 103:1-5 and write down three things you're thankful for today.

passages.why: "Enter His gates with thanksgiving."
"Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds."
"His loving devotion endures forever."
"Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in every circumstance."
Ten are healed; one comes back to say thank you.
"Rejoice in the Lord always."

title: How do I pray?
message: Prayer is simply talking with God, honestly. There's no special language required. When his disciples asked, "Lord, teach us to pray," Jesus gave them a short prayer we now call the Lord's Prayer. The Psalms are a whole book of prayers for every mood. Christian traditions pray in different ways, from set liturgies to silence to spontaneous words; all are welcome.
step: Pray the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9-13) slowly, pausing after each line to add your own words.

passages.why: Jesus teaches the Lord's Prayer.
"Ask, and it will be given to you."
"Pour out your hearts before Him."
When we don't know what to pray, "the Spirit Himself intercedes for us."
"In everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God."
God knows you already.

followUp.question: What makes prayer hard right now?

options.label: I don't know where to start

title: Looking for purpose or a big decision

terms: what should i do with my life

message: Questions of purpose and direction are big ones. The Bible doesn't usually give a detailed map for each decision, but it does give a direction: love God, love your neighbour, act justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Many Christians also find wisdom in prayer, Scripture and the advice of trusted people.
step: Read Micah 6:8 and Proverbs 3:5-6. Then talk your decision through with someone wise.

passages.why: "To act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God."
"Trust in the LORD with all your heart... He will make your paths straight."
The greatest commandments: love God and love your neighbour.
"Be transformed by the renewing of your mind."
Created "to do good works, which God prepared in advance."
God's promise to exiles: "plans to prosper you and not to harm you." (Spoken to Israel in exile.)

title: Relationships, love and marriage
message: Relationships bring some of life's deepest joy and deepest pain. The Bible celebrates love (it even contains a book of love poetry) and gives a picture of love that is patient and kind. If a relationship involves abuse or control, please know that is never God's will for you, and reach out for help.
step: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 and ask: where is love like this already, and where does it need help?

passages.why: "Love is patient, love is kind."
"It is not good for the man to be alone."
"Put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity."
"Wherever you go, I will go." A story of loyal love.
"Love is as strong as death... Mighty waters cannot quench love."
"He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds."

title: Family and parenting
message: Family life can be beautiful, messy and exhausting. The Bible is honest about families, including plenty of difficult ones, and returns again and again to God as a faithful parent. It encourages passing on faith in everyday life, and patience on all sides.
step: Read Luke 15:11-32 and notice how the father treats both of his sons.

passages.why: A father with two very different sons.
Talking about God's ways "when you sit at home and when you walk along the road."
"Unless the LORD builds the house..."
Children and parents, with gentleness.
Even Jesus' parents lost track of him and were anxious.
"As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you."

title: Temptation or addiction
message: Struggling with temptation or addiction is common, and nothing to hide from God. Paul wrote, "I do not do the good I want to do." Jesus was tempted too, so he understands. Real change usually needs support: a trusted friend, a church, a support group, or professional help.
step: Read 1 Corinthians 10:13 and Hebrews 4:15-16. Then tell one trustworthy person what you're facing.

passages.why: "God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear."
Jesus was tempted in every way, yet without sin; approach his throne of grace.
Jesus is tempted in the wilderness.
"I do not do the good I want to do."
Life by the Spirit, and the fruit of the Spirit.
How temptation grows, and the crown of life.

title: Money worries or job loss
message: Money worries can keep you awake at night. Jesus spoke about money more than almost any other topic, and he spoke gently to worried people: God knows what you need. The Bible also calls God's people to help those in need, so it's okay to ask for help.
step: Read Matthew 6:25-34, then write down one practical step and one thing you'll entrust to God.

passages.why: "Your heavenly Father knows that you need them."
"I am accustomed to any and every situation."
"My God will supply all your needs."
"Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content... Never will I leave you."
"Give me neither poverty nor riches."
"Never have I seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread."

options.label: I need to make a decision

title: Waiting for something
message: Waiting is hard, especially when you've prayed and nothing seems to change. The Bible is full of people who waited: Abraham and Sarah for a child, Israel in exile, the psalmists crying "How long?" Waiting on God is not passive; it's trusting him while you keep going.
step: Read Psalm 27:13-14 and Psalm 40:1-3.

passages.why: "Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous."
"I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry."
"Those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength."
"It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD."
"Though it lingers, wait for it."
Hope for what we do not yet see.

title: Looking for peace
message: Jesus promised his friends a peace that is different from what the world gives. In the Bible, peace (shalom) means more than calm: it means wholeness, everything as it should be. Stillness before God is a good place to start.
step: Read Psalm 46:10 and sit in silence for two minutes. Then read John 14:27.

passages.why: "Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you."
"The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding."
"You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind."
"The LORD bless you and keep you... and give you peace."
"I will lie down and sleep in peace."
"Be still, and know that I am God."

title: Facing something hard
message: Facing something hard takes courage, and the Bible's encouragement is not that you can do it on your own, but that you are not alone. Joshua, Esther and many others faced daunting challenges with that promise.
step: Read Joshua 1:9 before you go, and take it with you.

passages.why: "Be strong and courageous... for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."
"When you pass through the waters, I will be with you."
"The LORD is the stronghold of my life; whom shall I dread?"
"Who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
"I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength."
"He will never leave you nor forsake you."

title: Does God love me?
message: The Bible's answer is yes, more than you can imagine. "God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son." "God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us." God's love doesn't depend on how you feel or what you've done.
step: Read 1 John 4:9-10 and Romans 8:38-39. Try replacing "us" with your own name.

passages.why: "For God so loved the world..."
"While we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
"Not that we loved God, but that He loved us."
"He will rejoice over you with singing."
The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find the one.
Nothing "will be able to separate us from the love of God."

options.label: How can I be right with God?

title: Need some hope

terms: light at the end of the tunnel

message: Christian hope is not wishful thinking; it rests on God's faithfulness and on Jesus' resurrection. The Bible's story ends not in darkness but with God making all things new. Even in the middle of grief, the writer of Lamentations could say, "His mercies never fail. They are new every morning."
step: Read Lamentations 3:21-24, and come back to it tomorrow morning.

passages.why: "His mercies never fail. They are new every morning."
"May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace."
"A living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ."
"I wait for the LORD... and in His word I put my hope."
"Behold, I make all things new."
"Hope does not disappoint us."

options.label: To feel close to God again

title: How can I be right with God?
message: All Christian traditions agree that people are reconciled to God by his grace through Jesus Christ, and that this calls for faith and a changed life. They describe how that grace is received in different ways (for example, the roles of faith, baptism and the sacraments). The Bible passages below are ones all traditions treasure.
step: Read Luke 15:11-24 and Romans 5:1-8. If you want to take a step, talk to God honestly, and consider talking to a local church.

passages.why: "Everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life."
"All have sinned... and are justified freely by His grace."
"By grace you have been saved through faith."
"Repent and be baptized, every one of you."
"If you confess with your mouth, 'Jesus is Lord'..."
"He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy."

options.label: Which church is right for me?

title: Which church or tradition?

terms: why are there so many churches

message: There are many Christian traditions, from Catholic and Orthodox to many kinds of Protestant. They share a great deal (Jesus, the Bible, the creeds for most) and differ on questions like authority, baptism and Communion. Exploring them fairly, in their own words, can help you understand others and find where you belong.
step: Take the Belief Explorer quiz, then read the profiles of your top matches and their first-visit guides.

passages.why: Jesus prays "that all of them may be one."
"One Lord, one faith, one baptism."
What the first Christians did together.
Many parts, one body.

title: Questions about baptism or Communion
message: Baptism and Communion (the Lord's Supper) were given by Jesus and are practised by almost all Christians, but traditions understand them differently. Who should be baptised, and how? Is Jesus present in the bread and wine, and how? The Big Questions pages lay out each view fairly.
step: Read Matthew 28:18-20 and 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, then look at the two Big Questions below.

passages.why: Jesus sends his followers to baptise and teach.
Baptism as being buried and raised with Christ.
"Repent and be baptized."
The Last Supper: "Do this in remembrance of Me."
Paul passes on what he received about the Lord's Supper.
"Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life."

title: Mary and the saints
message: Mary, the mother of Jesus, is honoured by all Christians as a woman of great faith. Traditions differ on how she should be honoured and whether believers can ask her and the saints to pray for them. The passages below are where she appears in the Gospels and Acts.
step: Read Luke 1:26-56, Mary's response to the angel and her song.

passages.why: The angel Gabriel visits Mary: "I am the Lord's servant."
Mary's song (the Magnificat).
At the wedding in Cana: "Do whatever He tells you."
Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple.
Mary prays with the first disciples.

links.label: What is the role of Mary?

title: The Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts
message: Christians believe the Holy Spirit is God, present with believers, giving life, comfort and gifts. Traditions agree on much of this, but differ on whether gifts like speaking in tongues, prophecy and healing continue in the same way today.
step: Read Acts 2 (the day of Pentecost) and Galatians 5:22-23.

passages.why: Jesus promises "another Advocate", the Spirit of truth.
The Holy Spirit comes at Pentecost.
"The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children."
"There are different gifts, but the same Spirit."
The fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace...

links.label: Are the gifts of the Spirit for today?
